transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep messing up these little things. 

Like, I go down to the senior center—I usually go on Tuesdays, though they just moved the card games to Thursdays because Shirley at the front desk had to change her schedule to watch her grandson. Good kid, plays shortstop for the high school... but anyway, I'll be signing up for a class there and I just write down the completely wrong time on the sheet. 

Or I'll be out in the garage messing around with some wood. My dad was a carpenter, actually, built half the porches in our old neighborhood, always said "measure twice, cut once." But me, I'll measure a board, and I still end up cutting it a hair short because I just sort of... skip over the small print on the tape measure. And let me tell you, lumber is not cheap these days. I went down to the hardware store last week and I couldn't believe what they were charging for a simple two-by-four... but yeah, just silly mistakes like that.
Have you always struggled with these kinds of mistakes throughout your life, or is this something that has started happening more recently?

Oh, it's always been this way. Gosh, going way back. Even in elementary school... I went to Lincoln Elementary over on 4th street. Actually, they tore it down a few years ago to build that new strip mall, which is a real shame because they put in a mattress store, and honestly, how many mattresses do people in this town really need? There’s already three on the highway. 

But anyway, my teachers back then—like Mrs. Higgins, she was my third-grade teacher, always wore these thick glasses on a little pearl chain—they'd always write on my report cards that I was a bright boy, but I was constantly forgetting my books or losing my homework. And she wasn't wrong! I'd just be sitting at my desk staring out the window. They had these big old oak trees right outside the classroom, and I'd just watch the squirrels chasing each other up and down the branches all afternoon. Unless someone was standing right over me keeping me on track, I was just off in my own world. So, yeah, definitely not a new thing.
Growing up, did you often feel like you were driven by a motor, or did you find it difficult to stay seated when you were expected to?

No, not really. I never had that kind of... bouncy energy, you know? I was never the kid running around the classroom or jumping on the furniture. My brother, on the other hand, he was a holy terror. Tommy. He's three years younger than me, lives down in Florida now, near Tampa. He retired early, bought a boat, which I told him was a mistake because you know what they say about boats—a hole in the water you throw money into. And sure enough, the engine died on him his second time out, cost him a fortune to fix. But yeah, Tommy was the one who couldn't sit still. He broke my mother's good china vase once playing indoor baseball, which she had told him a hundred times not to do. But me? No, I was perfectly happy just sitting there. I'd sit at my desk, or on the porch, just... sitting. I wasn't causing trouble, I just wasn't doing what I was supposed to be doing either.
When you have a project or a task to complete, do you often find it difficult to organize the steps you need to take to get it done?

Oh, absolutely. Organization is... well, it's a real puzzle for me. Like, if I have a day where I need to run a few errands, maybe get the garage workshop ready for a project, and then I've got a doctor's appointment or something... I just can't seem to line them up right. I'll start getting the tools out, then remember I need to go to the post office, so I'll stop the workshop stuff, go find my keys... 

Speaking of the post office, they just changed their hours again. Used to be open till five, now they close the doors at four-thirty sharp. I found that out the hard way last Tuesday when I was trying to mail a birthday card to my niece, Sarah. She just turned thirty, which makes me feel ancient. She’s a physical therapist up in Seattle, loves it up there, says it doesn't rain as much as people think, but I don't know, every time I see her on video chat, she's wearing a raincoat. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll start one thing, stop, try to do another, and by the end of the day I'm just rushing around like a madman trying to get it all finished. It's like I can't figure out which piece of the puzzle goes first.
Do you often find that you lose things that are necessary for your tasks or activities, like your glasses, your wallet, or the tools you need for your projects?

Oh, constantly. It's ridiculous how much time I spend just hunting around the house for things. My keys, my reading glasses... my tape measure is a big one. I'll be out in the garage, and I'll have it right in my hand, set it down for a second, and then it's just gone. Like it sprouted legs! 

Same thing happens with this little bag of supplies I keep for my card games. I play Cribbage with some buddies down at the community center on Thursdays. Well, usually Thursdays, except last week they had to move us to Wednesday because the local theater troupe needed the main room for dress rehearsals. They're putting on Our Town. It's a classic, sure, but I swear they do it every three years. You'd think they'd try something new, maybe a comedy or a musical. My friend Arthur, he's actually in the play this year, plays the stage manager, and he was telling me the costumes they rented are just terribly itchy. He's got this wool vest that he says is driving him absolutely crazy under the stage lights... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the little bag of pegs and cards for Cribbage. I'll have it right in my hand getting ready to head out the door, put it down to grab my coat, and then I'm spending twenty minutes looking for it again even though I just held it a few minutes before. So, yeah, I definitely lose things more than I should.
In your day-to-day life, how often do you find yourself forgetting to keep appointments, pay bills, or follow through on the routine tasks you've planned for the day?

Well, honestly... I don't really think I have much trouble with that kind of stuff. I mean, my bills are all on that automatic payment thing the bank does now. My wife set it up before she passed, bless her heart. She was always the organized one. Used to keep this big wall calendar in the kitchen, right next to the fridge. It had pictures of lighthouses on it. She loved lighthouses. We took a trip up the coast of Maine once, back in... oh, it must have been '98, just driving from one lighthouse to the next. Beautiful country up there, but the food... I'll tell you, if you don't like lobster, you're out of luck. We went to this one place in Portland, and they served it with this drawn butter that was just... well, it was mostly just yellow grease, if you ask me. I ended up getting a hamburger, which the waitress looked at me like I had two heads for ordering. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, bills and appointments. Yeah, no, I don't really forget those. The dentist calls me the day before to remind me, and the auto pay handles the electric and the water. So I wouldn't say I forget those things, no.
Do you often find yourself feeling restless, like you need to be constantly moving or doing something, even if you aren't running around like a child?

Well, yeah, I'd say so. It's not like I'm running laps or anything, but I definitely get this... ants-in-my-pants feeling. Like, if I'm trying to have a quiet evening at the condo, or especially if I have to sit through a whole meeting. 

We have these homeowners association meetings at the condo complex, and they just drag on forever. Last month, they spent forty-five minutes arguing about the color of the mulch for the front flower beds. Forty-five minutes! Mrs. Higgins wanted this reddish cedar color, but the board president, Dave—he's a retired accountant, nice enough guy but a real stickler—he insisted on the dark brown because he said it matches the roofing tiles better. I mean, who looks at the roof and the dirt at the exact same time? And Dave is always wearing these loud Hawaiian shirts, which is just funny for a guy who's so obsessed with matching brown mulch... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the sitting. Yeah, sitting through that whole meeting, I just couldn't take it. I always end up wanting to get up, check something in the back of the room, or just leave and go putter around the garage. Even just during a quiet evening at home, watching a show, I get that same jittery feeling where I just need to stand up and fiddle with something.
